"Runic" means of, relating to, or written in runes. It describes anything connected to runes — the ancient carved letters of Northern European peoples. To truly understand "runic," you need to understand what runes are, so let's start there.

Runes are the characters of an ancient alphabet (actually a family of related alphabets) used by Germanic peoples — particularly the Vikings, Anglo-Saxons, and other Norse peoples — roughly from 200 AD onward, with some forms surviving even into the 1600s in Scandinavia.

What makes runes visually distinctive is that they look nothing like the smooth, curved letters you're reading right now. Runes are angular and geometric — think sharp strokes and straight lines with no curves. This is because they were designed to be carved into hard surfaces: stone, wood, bone, and metal. Carving curves into rock is difficult; straight lines are not. So the alphabet was shaped by its method of writing.

Each individual character in a runic alphabet is called a rune. The most famous runic alphabet is called the Elder Futhark, which has 24 such characters.
"Runic" carries two related but distinct meanings, and both are in active use today.

In its direct sense, "runic" simply means of or relating to actual historical runes. This is the technical use — used by historians, archaeologists, and linguists.

  • A runic inscription is text carved or written in runes.
  • A runic alphabet is any alphabet made of runic characters.
  • A runic stone (also called a runestone) is a stone bearing runic carving.
  • Runic script refers to runes treated as a writing system.

Example: "Runic inscriptions have been found across Scandinavia, the British Isles, and parts of Eastern Europe."
2. The figurative meaning: mysterious and cryptic

Here is where the word becomes richer. Runes were never just an alphabet. In the ancient world, they were believed to carry magical power. Warriors had runes carved onto their weapons to make them deadlier. People wore runic amulets for protection. Runes were connected to Odin, the Norse god of wisdom and war, who was said to have discovered them through great suffering. Because of this deep, historical association with secrecy, magic, and hidden knowledge, "runic" came to mean something beyond the alphabet itself: mysterious, cryptic, hard to read or interpret, and carrying a sense of hidden power.

When a writer uses "runic" figuratively, they mean something that:

  • Is deliberately obscure or hard to understand
  • Hints at hidden meaning beneath the surface
  • Carries an air of ancient mystery or secret knowledge

Examples:

  • "He gave a runic smile." — His smile seemed to conceal some secret; it was unreadable.
  • "Her instructions were runic." — Her instructions were so cryptic and unclear that no one could make sense of them.
  • "The old prophet spoke in runic riddles." — He spoke in deliberately obscure, mysterious language.

This figurative use appears often in literature, journalism, and academic writing.

Whether used literally or figuratively, "runic" almost always brings a particular atmosphere with it. It evokes:

  • Antiquity — something from a deep, distant past
  • Mystery — something not easily read or understood, like a code
  • Hidden power — the sense that this thing carries meaning beyond what is visible
  • The Norse world — carved stones in cold, windswept landscapes; ancient wisdom; old gods

This is precisely why "runic" is so widely used in fantasy literature and games. When a fantasy author writes about "runic markings" or a "runic blade," they are not necessarily referring to actual historical Norse runes. They are borrowing the atmosphere the word carries — the feeling of ancient, magical, encoded power. The word does heavy lifting just by being there.

It helps to know how "runic" sits alongside words that seem similar:

  • Cryptic means difficult to understand, but it has no historical or mystical weight — a cryptic crossword clue is just confusing.
  • Arcane means known only to a few; secretive or esoteric. It's closer to "runic" in feeling, but "arcane" suggests restricted knowledge, while "runic" suggests visually encoded or symbolically charged mystery.
  • Mystical suggests a connection to spiritual or supernatural forces, without the specific visual/written quality that "runic" carries.
  • Ancient just means old.

"Runic" is unique because it fuses the idea of a visual written symbol with mystery and ancient power. It is specific in a way the others are not.

• In history and archaeology: "The runestone bears a runic inscription dating to the 9th century."
  • In linguistics: "Old Norse was sometimes recorded in runic script."
  • In literature and fiction: "The cave walls were covered in glowing runic symbols, each one humming faintly with energy."
  • In metaphorical use: "He nodded with a runic expression, as though he alone understood what was coming."

"Runic" primarily means relating to runes — the angular, carved letters of ancient Germanic peoples, deeply associated with the Vikings and Norse culture. By natural extension, it also means mysterious, cryptic, or symbolically charged, because runes were historically tied to magic, hidden wisdom, and divine power. Whenever you encounter "runic," ask one question: is the writer referring to actual historical runes, or are they using the word to evoke a feeling of ancient mystery and encoded meaning? Both uses are correct, both are common, and once you know the connection between the two, the word will feel completely clear in any context.
